headline: US Farmers Embrace Trees and Grazing Despite Funding Cuts
meta_description: American farmers are adopting silvopasture—grazing livestock among trees—for climate and soil benefits, even as federal funding support shrinks.
summary_short: Farmers across the US are adopting silvopasture, pairing livestock with trees for healthier pastures and climate benefits, despite recent cuts to federal support program…
body:
Farmers across the United States are increasingly adopting silvopasture—an ancient ecological method that integrates grazing animals with woody perennials—even as federal financial supports for such climate-friendly practices falter. When Sabra Ewing and Sebastian Lousada purchased their Vermont dairy farm, they noticed their heritage sheep naturally gravitated toward the lusher grass growing beneath existing apple and maple trees. The observation sparked a transformation: today, Flag Hill Farm in Vershire grazes sheep under 80 varieties of apples alongside other useful trees, producing wool, hard cider, and brandy in an on-farm distillery. A recent USDA survey found that nearly a third of American farmers practicing agroforestry have adopted this livestock-centric variant, attracted by its capacity to improve forage quality while providing essential shade during increasingly hot and dry conditions.

The momentum is real, yet precarious. Grants from organizations like the American Farmland Trust and the USDA's Natural Resources Conservation Service proved essential for farms like Flag Hill and Howling Wolf Farm in nearby Randolph to establish their systems. Yet the current U.S. government froze the Partnership for Climate-Smart Commodities program, which had promised to invest up to $2.8 billion across 70 national projects. This matters because silvopasture requires 7 to 12 years before turning profitable—far longer than conventional annual crops—making upfront financial support critical.

What the funding cuts reveal is a deeper tension: silvopasture and agroforestry rank among agriculture's most effective methods for bolstering biodiversity and sequestering carbon. Once established, these systems produce sustained, increasing yields. Yet without government backing to bridge that long profitability gap, farmers struggle to compete with cheaper annual crop seeds. Meghan Giroux, director of Vermont nonprofit Interlace Commons, notes that recent NRCS policy changes have further complicated matters. The path forward, she emphasizes, requires a new farm bill that clarifies and strengthens these programs—ensuring that farmers' ecological innovations can take root.
quick_facts: Flag Hill Farm in Vermont grazes heritage sheep under 80 apple varieties
Nearly one-third of US agroforestry farmers practice silvopasture with livestock
Silvopasture takes 7–12 years to become profitable, requiring sustained support
Federal Climate-Smart Commodities program froze $2.8 billion in planned investments
